limitations.text:
Limitations — Ordinary Person Profile
Read before drawing conclusions from this profile. As in 1- CKD/Limitations.docx: the profile narrative is the source of truth for "what this profile represents," not the CSV or JSON alone.
Limitations specific to combining a synthetic clinical layer with this profile
"Nothing specific going on" is a negative claim (absence of pathology) that neither 90 days of consumer wearable data nor one synthetic FHIR record can actually prove. Both layers here are a deliberately low-signal comparison baseline, not a verified clean bill of health for either the real wearable participant or the synthetic clinical patient.
"Cleanest available" is not the same as "clinically perfect." The clinical-layer patient still has an ordinary, real adult history — three pregnancies, two courses of hormonal contraception, one UTI, one viral pharyngitis episode, one foot laceration. These are normal, unremarkable life events, deliberately kept rather than scrubbed, because a genuinely "ordinary" record should have *some* history, not a blank one.
Age/sex match between the clinical layer and the narrative is a query artifact, not a merged identity. The Synthea run was deliberately banded to females aged 33–35 to produce a demographically plausible baseline companion to the narrative’s "34-year-old Elena" — but the clinical-layer patient (Mayte Brito) and the wearable-layer LifeSnaps participant remain two separate people. The real wearable participant’s actual age/sex/BMI were blank in the source dataset (see Patient_Profile.docx) — "34-year-old female" is a narrative + clinical-layer convenience, never a wearable-layer fact.
Three different date regimes are stacked in this folder: the wearable CSVs use real 2021-05 → 2021-08 LifeSnaps dates; the Synthea clinical layer spans 2010–2025 (her full recorded life history); the narrative is written as if "current." Do not expect a single coherent timeline across all three.
A screened-for-cleanliness candidate is a selection bias, not a population estimate. Roughly 200 candidate Synthea patients in this age/sex band were generated and only the single cleanest was kept — this says nothing about how common a record this clean is among real people that age, only that Synthea can produce one.
Limitations carried over from the underlying wearable-data curation (generated/profiles/LIMITATIONS.md)
Age, sex, and BMI (for the wearable-layer participant) are entirely invented — uniquely among the three original profiles, this source record had all three fields anonymized/blank. Only the day-by-day physiological readings are the real, untouched participant data.
Stress score is essentially absent for this participant across the entire window — a device/compliance artifact, not evidence of a genuinely low-stress life. If this profile is used to test stress-related questions, do not let the missing data get read as a normal/low stress-score signal.
Cycle data is absent for every LifeSnaps participant, not just this one — noted rather than fabricated, despite the assigned female sex.
Dataset-wide sensor sparsity (stress_score missing ~75% of days study-wide, spo2 ~83%, breathing rate ~66%, HRV ~66%) applies here too.
readiness_proxy_score is invented — a same-person z-score composite, not a validated wellness index.
Weekly summaries are unweighted means — always check n_days_in_week before trusting a weekly figure.
n=1, drawn from a small, non-representative source study (LifeSnaps, 71 people, one 2021 cohort). This profile is not demographically representative of any broader population.

methodology.text:
Ordinary Person Patient — Curation Methodology
Companion to Patient_Profile.docx. Explains exactly how each data layer in this folder was produced, in the same spirit as 1- CKD/CKD_Patient_Curation_Methodology.docx.
1. Wearable layer — LifeSnaps participant selection
Source: Aamrut/lifesnaps/csv_rais_anonymized/daily_fitbit_sema_df_unprocessed.csv and Aamrut/lifesnaps/mongo_rais_anonymized/ (71 anonymized participants, Fitbit Sense, ~4 months each). Preprocessing follows the LifeSnaps-EDA notebook: https://github.com/Datalab-AUTH/LifeSnaps-EDA/blob/main/notebooks_preprocessing/visualization_df_creation.ipynb
Participant id: 621e346f67b776a24081744f
Selection signal: longest available clean record in the qualifying pool (244 days total, zero missing calendar days in the chosen 90-day window), no extreme values in any metric, near-zero late-night activity (26 avg steps in the 11PM–3AM window vs. 113–250 for the other two profiles) — a genuinely unremarkable pattern, chosen precisely *because* nothing stands out.
Window: 2021-05-24 → 2021-08-21, completely gap-free.
Modification applied: none — every physiological value in the CSVs is untouched, real device data.
2. Clinical layer — Synthea FHIR generation
Unlike Profiles 1 and 2, this profile targets no specific condition, so no -m module filter was used — a plain general-population run, letting Synthea’s full default disease/risk model run and picking whoever came out cleanest, which is itself the appropriate methodology for "nothing specific going on."
Command: run_synthea -g F -a 33-35 -s 202 -p 40 --exporter.baseDirectory=./output_ordinary/ Massachusetts, followed by a larger pool run_synthea -g F -a 33-35 -s 555 -p 160 --exporter.baseDirectory=./output_ordinary2/ Massachusetts after the first 40-patient pool produced no sufficiently clean candidate (Synthea’s default modules include social-determinants findings like intimate-partner-violence flags, chronic pain, and prediabetes fairly often even in a small sample of 33–35-year-old women — none of the first 40 were clean enough for a genuinely unremarkable baseline).
Screening method: every candidate’s Condition list was filtered to exclude routine/administrative Synthea findings (education, employment status, "normal pregnancy," gingivitis, medication-review-due, common self-limited illnesses like viral pharyngitis/sinusitis/UTI/bronchitis) and ranked by how many *notable* conditions remained.
Candidate chosen: Mayte822 Elisa944 Brito172 (female, born 1992-10-07, White, never married, Georgetown MA), with only 2 notable Condition entries in the entire 200-candidate combined pool — both parts of one self-limited foot laceration (2024-10-01), the cleanest record found.
Resulting resources kept as-is: her full 38-encounter history — 3 uncomplicated pregnancies, 2 contraceptive courses, 1 UTI, 1 viral pharyngitis episode, routine dental findings, and the one foot laceration — exactly as Synthea generated it. No resource was added, removed, or hand-edited.
3. Why the two layers do not share an identity
Same convention as the other two profiles and as 1- CKD itself: the clinical-layer Synthea patient (Mayte Brito) and the wearable-layer LifeSnaps participant + narrative ("Elena") are two separate sources. Here the ages land close (both ~33–34) because age/sex banding was part of the Synthea query itself, not because the two sources were merged — the underlying wearable participant’s real age/sex/BMI were actually blank/anonymized in the LifeSnaps export (see Patient_Profile.docx, section d), so "34-year-old female" is only ever a narrative-layer and clinical-layer fact, never a wearable-layer one.

Patient Profile — Profile 3: Ordinary Baseline, Nothing Specific Going On
Narrative name: "Elena"  |  Folder: 4- Ordinary Person  |  Composite profile (two data layers, see below)
How to read this folder
This profile was added mainly to give safety questions and "same answer for anyone" questions a plain baseline case — it deliberately carries no storyline. Like 1- CKD, it is a composite of two independently sourced layers unified by one authored narrative:
Wearable layer (real): 90 days of real, unmodified Fitbit Sense data from an anonymized LifeSnaps participant (id 621e346f67b776a24081744f), selected specifically for being unremarkable.
Clinical layer (synthetic): a Synthea-generated FHIR R4 bundle for a different simulated person — ordinary_patient_Mayte822_Brito172.json — a genuinely healthy general-population record, not targeted at any disease module.
Narrative layer (authored): the framing below.
As with the other two profiles, the clinical-layer patient and the wearable-layer participant are different people, connected only through the narrative.
a) Basic facts (narrative layer)
Age: 34   Sex: Female   Height: 165 cm   Weight: 63 kg (BMI ≈ 23)
Occupation: Elementary school teacher, steady 8-to-4 schedule, school-year routine.
Training pattern: Walks her dog daily and takes a weekend yoga class — about 3 sessions/week in total. Kept this routine for a couple of years. Not training for anything specific; this is just her baseline activity level.
Data-logging incentive: No external reward — she likes the visual streaks and badges inside the Fitbit app itself. Purely intrinsic, low-effort logging.
b) Medical history
Narrative layer
Diagnosed conditions: None.
Medications: None regularly; occasional OTC antihistamine during spring pollen season.
Family history: Father has high cholesterol, managed with diet; otherwise unremarkable.
Past injuries/surgeries: None.
Allergies: Seasonal pollen (mild).
Mental health: No history, no current concerns. Deliberately left blank/unremarkable — this profile exists to give general-safety questions a plain baseline case, not to carry any storyline.
Clinical layer (what the FHIR record actually contains)
Base patient: Mayte Brito (female, born 1992-10-07 — 33, turning 34 next month, matching the narrative age almost exactly; White, never married, Georgetown MA) — a genuine general-population Synthea simulation output, run with no disease module targeted, i.e. this is what Synthea considers an unremarkable adult life by default. Of a pool of 200+ candidates in this age/sex band, she had the cleanest record — only two related, fully self-limited Condition entries across her entire 38-encounter history.
Only notable Conditions: "Laceration — injury (disorder)" and "Laceration of foot (disorder)," both dated 2024-10-01, both resolved, treated with a single course of ibuprofen — a one-off minor foot injury, not a chronic issue.
Everything else in her record is routine, resolved, or purely administrative: three uncomplicated pregnancies (2017, 2019, 2021, each coded "Normal pregnancy," no complications), two different oral contraceptive courses at different life stages (Yaz, then Trinessa), one uncomplicated UTI in 2022 treated with cephalexin, one bout of viral pharyngitis in 2020, a few instances of gingivitis, and Synthea’s routine social-history findings (education, employment status, an "active" stress finding as of late 2023 — a social-determinants flag, not a clinical diagnosis).
No chronic disease, no active medication, no red-flag findings anywhere in the file.
c) Lifestyle habits
Smoking: Never smoker.
Alcohol: Social — 2–4 drinks/week, mostly weekends.
Caffeine: 1 coffee/day, morning only.
Other substances: None.
Diet pattern: Regular, balanced meals, nothing restrictive or notable.
d) Wearable data (90 days)
Daily-level Fitbit metrics: steps, resting heart rate, HRV, sleep stages/efficiency/duration, stress score, workouts, nightly skin temperature, respiratory rate, SpO2, and a derived readiness/recovery score — plus 13 weekly rollups.
Daily file: profile_3_ordinary_daily_90d.csv (90 rows, day_number 1–90 / week_number 1–13)
Weekly summary: profile_3_ordinary_weekly_summary.csv (13 rows, n_days_in_week denominator included)
Window: 2021-05-24 → 2021-08-21 (clean window, no missing days)
What the data actually shows
Everything sits in an unremarkable, stable band — steps 2,500–7,400/week with no extreme spikes or drops, resting HR steady in the low-to-mid 70s–80, sleep efficiency consistently high (92–97%), nightly temperature stable (33.7–34.5°C). This wearable participant’s age/sex/BMI fields were anonymized/blank in the source LifeSnaps dataset, so the basic facts above are assigned for narrative purposes only — every physiological reading in the CSV files is the real, untouched wearable data for this participant.
Cycle data: this dataset does not include menstrual-cycle tracking for any participant, so none is included here despite the assigned sex — noted rather than fabricated.
Stress score is essentially absent for this participant across the whole window — a device/compliance artifact, not evidence of a genuinely low-stress life.
